sentences.text: She found the web in the June, about four metres off the path, spun between two hornbeam trunks at head height, and she found it by walking into the edge of it and getting it across her mouth.
She was not looking for a web.

She was looking for a surface — a rock face, a change in the ground, anything that could bounce or absorb — and she had been four metres off the path on the uphill side because that is where the trunks are thickest.
It is not a normal web and it is not a beautiful one.
It is a rough sheet, perhaps two metres across, sagging in the middle, grey and slightly furred, with no radiating pattern at all — nothing like the wheel you get from a garden spider.
Somebody who did not live there would take it for old cobweb and dust.
There is a spider.
She is small and brown and unremarkable and Iva has seen her perhaps six times in eleven years, always at the top left, always still.

Iva has photographed her twice and shown the photographs to one entomologist, at a fair in Nova Gorica, who looked at them for a while and said it was probably a *Tegenaria* and that the web was atypical and that the photographs were not good enough, all of which was fair.
And the web catches sound.
Iva established this over that summer with a method she is still, at twenty-four, moderately pleased with.
She clapped at measured distances and recorded.
She did it in June, in July, in the first week of August, and in the last.
In June a clap from four metres came back off the recording thin but present.
By the end of August a clap from four metres was not on the recording at all.
Not quiet — absent.
The microphone got the click of her own jaw and the birds and no clap whatsoever.
She did it eleven times in the last week of August because she assumed the phone was faulty.
She did it with a different phone.
She got her cousin to clap while she held the phone, in case the problem was that the sound and the microphone were in the same place.
Nothing.

Birds, wind, the stream from beyond the line, her cousin saying *now?* — which recorded perfectly well, because her cousin was standing outside the hornbeams — and then a silence exactly where the clap went.
The web was, by then, visibly loaded.
It had gone from grey to a darker grey and it sagged about a hand's width lower in the middle and it did not move in the wind the way it had in June.
There is nothing in it.
That has to be said, because everybody assumes there must be something visible.
She has looked at that sheet from twenty centimetres with a torch in August and it is empty — no flies, no husks, no wrapped parcels.
It is a grey sheet that has become heavier without acquiring anything.
That is the whole phenomenon and it is not, on its own, especially frightening.
The frightening part is what everybody in Podgora knows about September.
